This page documents the columns, dtypes and units returned by each dataset. The frames shown are produced by executing the code when the page is built, so they correspond to the current contents of the package.

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True).drop(columns='license')
```

Licenses are omitted here for width; they are listed in [Provenance](provenance.qmd), and in full in `NOTICE.md`.

## Demographics

Five series are taken from UN World Population Prospects 2024, Medium variant. They are grouped in a single store and versioned by WPP revision, and consist of decadal snapshots from 1950 to 2100, giving sixteen time points. All 187 countries have all five series.

The column names follow the UN's own conventions, so the frames can be passed to Starsim's demographic modules without renaming anything.

### Births and migration

Both are national rates with one value per year and no age dimension. The UN publishes no age breakdown for migration; births by age of mother are the `fertility` series, below.

```{python}
births = ssd.load('kenya', which='births')
births.head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(column='Time', dtype='int64', units='calendar year', note='decadal, 1950-2100'),
    dict(column='CBR', dtype='float32', units='births per 1,000 population per year', note=''),
])
```

The `migration` series has the same shape, with `CNMR` (crude net-migration rate per 1,000) in place of `CBR`. It is signed, with negative values indicating net emigration.

```{python}
ssd.load('kenya', which='migration').head(3)
```

### Deaths

Age- and sex-specific mortality, in 5-year abridged bins (`0`, `1–4`, `5–9`, …, `100+`). Only Female and Male are retained; the UN's "Both sexes" rows are dropped, which matches Starsim's sex conventions.

```{python}
deaths = ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths')
deaths.head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(column='Time', dtype='int64', units='calendar year', note=''),
    dict(column='Sex', dtype='string', units='Female | Male', note='no "Both sexes"'),
    dict(column='AgeGrpStart', dtype='int64', units='years', note='start of the bin: 0, 1, 5, 10, ..., 100'),
    dict(column='mx', dtype='float32', units='deaths per person-year', note='the central death rate m(x)'),
])
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Death rates are not probabilities
`mx` is the central death rate, meaning deaths per person-year of exposure, rather than the probability of dying during the interval (`qx`). The two are similar where mortality is low and diverge where it is high. The remaining life-table columns are available through `fetch()`, as described below.
:::

```{python}
len(deaths), deaths.Time.nunique(), deaths.AgeGrpStart.nunique()
```

This is sixteen years multiplied by two sexes and twenty-two age bins.

### Population

Population counts by 5-year age group and sex, expressed as absolute persons. The UN's own CSV distributions express these in thousands; the conversion is applied when the store is built.

```{python}
population = ssd.load('kenya', which='population')
population.head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(column='Time', dtype='int64', units='calendar year', note=''),
    dict(column='Sex', dtype='string', units='Female | Male', note=''),
    dict(column='AgeGrp', dtype='int64', units='years', note='start of the bin: 0, 5, ..., 100'),
    dict(column='Value', dtype='float32', units='persons', note='absolute count, not thousands'),
])
```

The national total provides a check on the units:

```{python}
f"{population[population.Time == 2020].Value.sum() / 1e6:.1f}M"
```

### Fertility

Age-specific fertility rates, by 5-year age group of the mother (`10–14`, …, `50–54`). There is no `Sex` column, since the rates are per woman.

```{python}
fertility = ssd.load('kenya', which='fertility')
fertility.head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(column='Time', dtype='int64', units='calendar year', note=''),
    dict(column='AgeGrpStart', dtype='int64', units='years', note='start of the bin: 10, 15, ..., 50'),
    dict(column='ASFR', dtype='float32', units='births per 1,000 women per year', note='the age-specific fertility rate'),
])
```

Summed over the age groups, times five years per group and divided by 1,000, it gives the total fertility rate:

```{python}
f"{5 * fertility[fertility.Time == 2020].ASFR.sum() / 1000:.2f}"
```

### Revisions

Demographic stores are versioned by WPP revision, so that a new UN release adds a store rather than altering data already in use:

```{python}
ssd.list_revisions()
```

```python
ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths')                 # newest bundled revision
ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths', revision=2024)  # pinned
```

Pinning the revision is advisable in any analysis intended to be reproduced later.

## Contact matrices

Contact matrices give the average number of daily contacts between people in each pair of age bins. Three sources are available, each providing five contact settings, selected with the `kind` argument. One of them, `prem2021`, is bundled; the other two are fetched on first use (see [Bundled, fetched and downloaded data](access.qmd)). The default, `prem`, is `prem2021`, or `prem2017` for the ten locations `prem2021` lacks (see [Which source](#which-source)).

```{python}
matrix = ssd.load('kenya')   # prem2021
matrix.iloc[:6, :6].round(3)
```

The frames are square and `float32`, and both axes are indexed by the start age of the bin rather than by position, which permits selection by age:

```{python}
matrix.loc[25, 30]
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(source='prem', access='bundled', shape='16x16', bins='5-year, 0-4 ... 75+',
         countries=187, study='prem2021, with prem2017 for the ten locations it lacks'),
    dict(source='prem2021', access='bundled', shape='16x16', bins='5-year, 0-4 ... 75+',
         countries=177, study='Prem et al. 2021'),
    dict(source='prem2017', access='fetched', shape='16x16', bins='5-year, 0-4 ... 75+',
         countries=152, study='Prem et al. 2017'),
    dict(source='mistry2021', access='fetched', shape='85x85', bins='single-year, 0 ... 84+',
         countries=36, study='Mistry et al. 2021'),
    dict(source='mistry2021_us', access='fetched', shape='85x85', bins='single-year, 0 ... 84+',
         countries='51 US states (with DC)', study='Mistry et al. 2021'),
])
```

The `kind` argument selects the setting:

```{python}
{kind: round(float(ssd.load('kenya', kind=kind).to_numpy().sum()), 1)
 for kind in ('all', 'home', 'work', 'school', 'community')}
```

The `all` matrix is the combined one and the remaining four are its components, although they do not sum exactly to `all`, since the upstream sources construct them separately.

Coverage differs between sources, and is worth checking before use. The locations of a fetched source are listed without downloading it:

```{python}
len(ssd.list_locations('prem2021')), len(ssd.list_locations('prem2017')), len(ssd.list_locations('mistry2021'))
```

The other two sources are read with `fetch()`, which downloads each store once (about 3 MB) and returns exactly the frame `load()` would:

```python
ssd.fetch('japan', which='prem2017', kind='home')   # 16x16
ssd.fetch('france', which='mistry2021')             # 85x85, single years of age
```

### Which source

`prem2021` is the authors' own update of `prem2017`, built from more contact surveys and newer demographic data, and covering 177 locations against 152. Where both have a country, they agree closely: the median correlation between a country's two matrices is 0.957.

`prem2021` dropped ten locations that `prem2017` has: Andorra, Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, Haiti, Japan, Kiribati, Lebanon, Monaco, Seychelles and Taiwan. Their `prem2017` matrices are bundled too, and the default contact matrices, `prem`, use them, so `ssd.load()` has a matrix for all 187 locations. Which study a frame came from is recorded on it:

```{python}
ssd.load('Japan').attrs['dataset']
```

Asking for `prem2021` by name gives that study alone, and says where else a location can be found:

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.load('Japan', which='prem2021')
```

The full `prem2017` is fetched for reproducing earlier analyses. `mistry2021` answers a different need: single-year age bins, but for only 36 mostly high-income countries, under the more permissive Apache-2.0 license.

### US states

`mistry2021_us` has the Mistry et al. 2021 matrices for each US state and the District of Columbia, and `population_us` each one's population in 2023 by single year of age, from the US Census Bureau, in the same age bins. A state is named with its country, separated by a colon, as in the node table's `dot_name` (see [Locations](locations.qmd#subnational-units)):

```{python}
ssd.list_locations('mistry2021_us')[:3]
```

```python
ssd.fetch('United States:Massachusetts', which='mistry2021_us', kind='school') # 85x85
ssd.fetch('United States:Massachusetts', which='population_us') # Time, Sex, AgeGrp, Value
```

`population_us` has the columns of `population`, for the one year 2023 and with `Sex` equal to `'Both sexes'`, since the source does not split by sex. The national datasets say where a state's data is:

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.load('United States:Massachusetts')
```

## The node table

The node table contains one row per administrative unit. It is described in full in [Spatial data](spatial.qmd); the schema is reproduced here for completeness.

```{python}
nodes = ssd.load_nodes('kenya', level=1)
nodes.head(3)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame([
    dict(column='nodeid', dtype='int32', note='0-based within (location, level); indexes the distance matrix'),
    dict(column='location', dtype='str', note='canonical location key, e.g. Kenya'),
    dict(column='iso3', dtype='str', note='ISO 3166-1 alpha-3'),
    dict(column='level', dtype='int32', note='0 = country, 1 = first-level subdivision'),
    dict(column='name', dtype='str', note="the unit's own name, as the source spells it"),
    dict(column='pcode', dtype='str', note='the join key: a p-code for UNOCHA rows, a shapeID otherwise'),
    dict(column='dot_name', dtype='str', note='hierarchical path, e.g. Kenya:Baringo'),
    dict(column='parent', dtype='str', note="the parent's dot_name; empty at level 0"),
    dict(column='lat', dtype='float64', note='equal-area centroid latitude, WGS84'),
    dict(column='lon', dtype='float64', note='equal-area centroid longitude, WGS84'),
    dict(column='area_km2', dtype='float64', note='geodesic area on the WGS84 ellipsoid'),
    dict(column='population', dtype='float64', note='UN WPP at level 0; WorldPop 2020 summed within each unit at level 1'),
    dict(column='source', dtype='str', note='unocha or geoboundaries'),
])
```

## Beyond the bundle

For the five bundled series, `fetch()` returns the same schema at annual resolution, and for the contact sources that are not bundled (`prem2017`, `mistry2021` and `mistry2021_us`) the same frame `load()` returns for `prem2021`. It also provides two datasets with no bundled counterpart:

```{python}
ssd.list_fetchable()
```

```python
ssd.fetch('kenya', which='deaths', years=(2000, 2025))
```

| Returns | Columns |
|---|---|
| `births`, `migration` | as bundled, but every year |
| `deaths`, `population`, `fertility` | as bundled, but every year |
| `life_table` | `Time, Sex, AgeGrpStart, mx, qx, px, lx, dx, Lx, Sx, Tx, ex, ax` — and all three sexes, including `Total` |
| `indicators` | `Time` plus ~50 WPP indicators: `CDR`, `TFR`, `LEx`, `IMR`, `Q5`, `NetMigrations`, … |

The `life_table` result carries a glossary of its columns, since the conventional two-letter names are easily confused:

```python
lt = ssd.fetch('kenya', which='life_table', years=2020)
lt.attrs['columns']['Lx']
# 'person-years lived between ages x and x+n'
```

## What is not here

- **Subnational demographics,** other than the populations of the US states (`population_us`, above). WPP has no subnational dimension, so none can be derived from it.
- **Age-specific migration.** WPP publishes only the crude national rate.
- **"Both sexes" rows** in the bundled series, which contain Female and Male only. `fetch('life_table')` does include `Total`.
- **Hong Kong, Macao and Puerto Rico** in the node table, as no boundary source covers them as separate entities. Their demographics and contact matrices are present.
